title: Deep in one: the Gospel of Mark
for: I want to know one book well
subtitle: Sixteen sessions, one for each chapter of Mark, the shortest Gospel: read the chapter and its notes, and follow the book's own shape from the river to the cross and the empty tomb.
intro: This track reads one book of the Bible slowly, a chapter at a sitting. Mark is the shortest of the four Gospels, most scholars think it the earliest, and it moves fast, from a voice in the wilderness to an empty tomb in sixteen chapters. Each session takes about fifteen minutes: read the chapter, then its notes in plain words, then come back to one question, one thing to do, and one verse.

If you can, read the whole book once in an evening before you begin, as its first hearers did, then come back here and take it slowly. The track follows Mark's own shape: the question of who Jesus is, his habit of telling people to keep quiet, the road to Jerusalem, and an ending the oldest manuscripts don't share with the later ones. Each session ends with a guide for a group.

sessions.title: The beginning of the gospel
teaching: Mark opens with a title, “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (Mark 1:1), and then he runs. There is no birth story. John appears in the wilderness dressed like Elijah, Jesus comes up out of the Jordan and sees the heavens torn open, the Spirit drives him into the desert, and by verse 15 he is announcing that the time is fulfilled. Watch the word translated ‘immediately’ or ‘at once’. Mark uses it about forty times in the book, eleven of them in this chapter.

Notice that the reader is told who Jesus is in the first line, and the voice from heaven says it again at his baptism, but hardly anyone in the story knows. The unclean spirit in the synagogue knows, and Jesus silences it. The man with leprosy is healed and told to say nothing, and he tells everyone. These are the first of the commands to keep quiet that run through the book, a pattern called the messianic secret since William Wrede's study of 1901. The reader knows the answer, and the drama is watching the people in the story struggle toward it.

open.label: Mark 1, passage by passage
open.why: Each passage of the first chapter explained in plain words, with what its first hearers would have noticed and the hard questions it raises.

also.label: Mark's introduction in the Study Bible
also.why: Who wrote Mark, when and for whom, how the book is built, and how to read it in one sitting.

also.label: Who Jesus is
also.why: Seven short pictures of who Christians confess Jesus to be, ending with the question he asked his friends near Caesarea Philippi.

sessions.question: What does Mark want you to know about Jesus before anyone in the story knows it, and why might he tell you first?
sessions.do: Before the next session, read the whole of Mark in one sitting if you can, aloud or with a recording, without stopping to look anything up. It takes about as long as a film. Note every time someone asks who Jesus is.

verse.text: And a voice came from heaven: “You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.”

group.open: Have you ever read a whole book of the Bible in one sitting? What was it like, or what do you imagine it would be like?
discuss: Mark starts with John in the wilderness and no birth story. What does that opening tell you about the kind of book this is?
The spirit in the synagogue knows who Jesus is, and Jesus tells it to be silent. Why might he refuse a true word from that source?
The man with leprosy is sure Jesus can help and unsure that he wants to. Why do you think Jesus touches him before he heals him?
group.pray: Give thanks in your own words for one thing you saw in Jesus in this chapter, and ask that each person in the group would read the whole book with open eyes.

sessions.title: Authority to forgive
teaching: Chapter 2 is a chain of arguments, and the first is the sharpest. Four friends dig through a roof and lower a man who cannot walk, and Jesus says, “Son, your sins are forgiven” (Mark 2:5). The scribes ask the right question: who can forgive sins but God alone? They are not being petty. Only God can forgive what is done against God. Jesus doesn't correct their logic. He heals the man so that they may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive, and this is the first time in Mark he calls himself by that name.

Then the arguments keep coming, each one about what Jesus does with the people and customs around him. He calls a tax collector from his booth and eats with people the respectable kept at a distance. He says his disciples can't fast while the bridegroom is with them, and inside that picture Mark slips the first hint that the bridegroom will be taken away. He defends hungry disciples on the Sabbath and calls himself its Lord. A reader can watch the opposition grow from a question in the heart to the plot that comes at the start of chapter 3.

open.label: Mark 2, passage by passage
open.why: A roof dug through, a tax collector called, a wedding with no fasting and grain picked on the Sabbath, each passage explained in plain words.

also.label: Was Jesus just a good teacher?
also.why: It begins with this scene in Mark 2 and asks why the respectable verdict on Jesus is the one the earliest sources make hardest to hold.

sessions.question: The scribes asked who can forgive sins but God alone. How would you answer them?
sessions.do: Read Mark 2:1-12 again slowly and write down every person in the room and what each one wants. Then read the note on the hard question below the passage.

verse.text: On hearing this, Jesus told them, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who are the people you would least expect to find at a famous teacher's dinner table today?
discuss: The friends came for healing, and Jesus spoke first of forgiveness. Why do you think he started there?
The scribes' logic was sound. If they were right that only God forgives sins, what is Jesus claiming?
Jesus says it is the sick who need a doctor. What keeps people from admitting they are the sick ones?
group.pray: Give thanks that forgiveness is offered, and pray for one person each of you knows who feels too far gone to be welcome at the table.

sessions.title: A new family
teaching: Chapter 3 begins with a withered hand made whole on the Sabbath, and the healing ends in a plot: the Pharisees go out and begin plotting with the Herodians how they might kill Jesus. Then Mark arranges the people around him. Jesus goes up a mountain and appoints twelve, a number every Jewish hearer would connect with Israel's twelve tribes. His own family sets out to take custody of him, because people are saying he is out of his mind. Scribes from Jerusalem say his power comes from the prince of demons.

Watch how Mark tells it. He starts the family's story, sets the scribes' accusation in the middle, and then finishes the family's story, a habit of his that readers call a sandwich, where each half explains the other. When his mother and brothers arrive, they stand outside and send for him. Jesus looks at the people sitting in a circle around him and says that whoever does the will of God is his brother and sister and mother. The line between inside and outside doesn't run through blood. It runs between those who sit near and listen and those who stay back.

open.label: Mark 3, passage by passage
open.why: A healing that starts a plot, the Twelve appointed, a family that thinks him mad, and the warning about blasphemy, each explained in plain words.

also.label: What the church is
also.why: Seven pictures of the family Jesus was gathering: a people, one body, living stones, and what churches share where they differ.

sessions.question: Where do you stand in this chapter: in the circle around Jesus, outside asking him to come out, or watching from a distance?
sessions.do: Read 3:20-35 as one story, the family, the scribes, then the family again, and notice how each part explains the other. Then read the note on 3:22-30, which takes up the warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit and the fear many people carry about it.

verse.text: For whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother.

care: If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What did your family think when you, or someone close to you, started to take faith seriously?
discuss: Jesus' own family thought he was out of his mind. Why do you think Mark kept that detail?
The scribes saw the same healings as the crowd and drew the opposite conclusion. What does that say about evidence and the heart?
Jesus counts as family everyone who does the will of God. What would it take for a church to feel like that family?
group.pray: Pray for your own families by name, especially where faith divides them, and give thanks for the family Jesus is still gathering.

sessions.title: Seeds and a storm
teaching: In chapter 4 Jesus teaches from a boat in parables, short stories from ordinary life that leave the hearer to finish the thought. A farmer throws seed everywhere, three kinds of ground fail, and the fourth gives a harvest far bigger than the losses. A lamp is meant for a stand. A seed grows while the farmer sleeps, and he doesn't know how. The smallest seed becomes a plant the birds can nest in. Each picture says that God's kingdom starts small and hidden and grows by God's power, and each one turns back on the listener and asks how you hear.

Then the same boat crosses the lake at night. A storm fills it while Jesus sleeps on a cushion in the stern, and the disciples wake him with a question that is more than panic: “Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?” (Mark 4:38). He rebukes the wind and tells the sea to be silent, with the same words he used on the unclean spirit in the synagogue. Mark notes a great storm, a great calm and then great fear. The disciples end the chapter asking the book's own question: who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

open.label: Mark 4, passage by passage
open.why: The farmer and the seed, why Jesus spoke in parables, the seed that grows by itself, and the storm on the lake, each explained in plain words.

also.label: The kingdom of God
also.why: Seven pictures of what Jesus meant by the kingdom: God's rule come near, its signs, the mustard seed, and why it is here and not yet complete.

sessions.question: Which kind of ground do you recognize in yourself this week, and what is crowding the seed?
sessions.do: Read 4:35-41 aloud and stop at the disciples' question to Jesus. Write down whether your own hardest question for God is about his power or about whether he cares.

verse.text: Overwhelmed with fear, they asked one another, “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?”

care: This passage is not a rebuke of people who live with an anxiety disorder, panic attacks or depression. Those are real illnesses of body and mind, and they need care, not blame. Getting help is not a lack of faith, and nothing in this verse forbids it. A doctor, a counselor, medicine, one trusted person who will stay can all be part of how God cares for you. The Honest Answer ‘Is my anxiety a spiritual failure?’ says more. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Have you ever been caught in weather, or in a moment, when you were sure you were not going to make it?
discuss: Three kinds of ground fail and one gives a huge harvest. Is the parable more of a warning or a promise?
The disciples asked whether Jesus cared. Why is that a different question from whether he could help?
After the calm the disciples are more afraid than before. Why might the calm frighten them more than the storm did?
group.pray: Name one storm each of you is in, and pray for one another, asking that each person would trust that Jesus cares as well as that he can help.

sessions.title: Three people past hope
teaching: Chapter 5 brings Jesus to three people no one else could help. Across the lake, in Gentile country, a man lives among the tombs, breaking every chain and cutting himself with stones. Jesus sets him free, and the town is more afraid of the man sitting calm and clothed than it ever was of the man in chains. Back on the Jewish side, a synagogue leader named Jairus falls at Jesus' feet for his dying daughter, and on the way a woman who has been ill for twelve years touches his cloak from behind.

Mark wraps the woman's story inside the girl's, so that each explains the other. Both are called daughter. The woman has been ill twelve years, and the girl is twelve years old. While Jesus stops for the woman, word comes that the girl has died, and he says to her father, “Do not be afraid; just believe” (Mark 5:36). Mark keeps the very words Jesus spoke to the girl in Aramaic, “Talitha koum!” (Mark 5:41), and then he remembers that she needs something to eat. Nothing that holds a person, however strong, is stronger than Jesus.

open.label: Mark 5, passage by passage
open.why: A man called Legion, a woman who touched his cloak and a girl who was not dead but asleep, each passage explained in plain words.

also.label: What Does the Bible Say About What I Am Facing?
also.why: If one of these three stories is close to your own, say what you are facing in your own words and read the passages that bear on it.

sessions.question: Which of the three people in this chapter is closest to where you are, and what would you ask Jesus for?
sessions.do: Read 5:21-43 in one sitting, the girl's story with the woman's inside it. Write down every place where the two stories echo each other.

verse.text: But Jesus overheard their conversation and said to Jairus, “Do not be afraid; just believe.”

care: It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, or you feel you do not want to go on, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. You do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who do you know who has been written off as too far gone?
discuss: The town asked Jesus to leave after the man was set free. Why might a rescue that costs something be unwelcome?
The woman wanted help without being seen, and Jesus called her forward. Why didn't he let her slip away?
Between the bad news and the miracle, Jesus gives Jairus one sentence. What would it mean to keep walking with that sentence?
group.pray: Pray by name for people each of you knows who seem past hope, and for anyone in the group who is waiting on news.

sessions.title: Bread in the wilderness
teaching: Chapter 6 begins with rejection at home. In Nazareth the people who watched Jesus grow up ask where a carpenter got all this, and they take offense. Then Mark makes another sandwich. Jesus sends the Twelve out two by two, and before they come back Mark tells how Herod had John the Baptist beheaded at a birthday feast. Those who preach repentance, as John did, may meet John's end, and his execution casts its shadow ahead toward Jesus' own: a ruler who knows the man is holy, guests to please, and a body laid in a tomb by his followers.

When the apostles return, a crowd follows them to a solitary place, the same word Mark used for the wilderness, and Jesus has compassion on them as sheep without a shepherd. He teaches them, then tells his disciples to feed them. Five loaves become enough for five thousand men, with twelve baskets left over, and the four things he does with the bread, taking, blessing, breaking and giving, will come back at his last supper. That night he comes to the disciples walking on the sea, and Mark says plainly that they had not understood about the loaves.

open.label: Mark 6, passage by passage
open.why: Rejected at home, the Twelve sent out, John's death, five thousand fed and Jesus on the water, each passage explained in plain words.

also.label: The guided study of Mark 6
also.why: The same chapter in seven steps, one screen at a time, and it keeps your place. Closing it shows the way back to this session.

sessions.question: What small thing do you have that Jesus might ask you to bring, the way the disciples brought five loaves?
sessions.do: Work through the guided study of this chapter as far as its hard question. Then write down what you think the disciples had failed to understand about the loaves.

verse.text: When Jesus stepped ashore and saw a large crowd, He had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And He began to teach them many things.

group.open: When has an interruption turned out to be the most important part of your day?
discuss: The people of Nazareth thought they already knew Jesus. How can being familiar with him keep someone from seeing him?
Why do you think Mark tells the story of John's execution in the middle of the disciples' mission?
Jesus told the disciples to give the crowd something to eat themselves. What does that ask of a church today?
group.pray: Give thanks for the ways God has provided for each of you, and ask him to use whatever small thing each person has to bring this week.

sessions.title: What makes a person unclean
teaching: Chapter 7 begins with a complaint from Jerusalem: some of Jesus' disciples eat without washing their hands in the proper religious way. Mark stops to explain the custom, because many of his readers were not Jews. The washing was about being fit to come near God, and devout people were trying to live with the holiness of priests. Jesus answers with Isaiah's words about people who honor God with their lips while their hearts are far away, and with the example of a vow called Corban that let a man keep money back from his own father and mother.

Then he moves the question from the plate to the heart. Nothing that goes into a person from outside makes him unclean. What comes out of the heart does, and Jesus names it: evil thoughts, theft, greed, deceit, envy, arrogance and more. Mark adds his own comment, that this made all foods clean, and Christians read what Jesus meant by it in more than one way. Then the chapter goes into Gentile country, where a mother from Syria answers Jesus back and wins, and a deaf man is healed with one Aramaic word, Ephphatha, “Be opened!” (Mark 7:34).

open.label: Mark 7, passage by passage
open.why: Unwashed hands, what really makes a person unclean, the woman who answered back, and a deaf man who hears, each explained in plain words.

also.label: What sin is
also.why: Six pictures of sin at its root, the four things it breaks, why it touches everyone, and the God who comes looking.

sessions.question: Where do you guard the outside of your life while leaving the heart alone?
sessions.do: Read Jesus' list in 7:21-23 slowly. Choose one thing on it that you recognize in yourself, and bring it to God in plain words instead of only guarding the doors against it.

verse.text: Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him; but the things that come out of a man, these are what defile him.

care: Some people are troubled by unwanted thoughts that come again and again, often about the very things they most fear or hate. If that is you, hear this gently. Having such a thought is not the same as choosing it, and it is not sin. Trying harder to ‘capture’ it often makes it louder. This can be part of anxiety or obsessive-compulsive disorder, and it can be treated. A doctor or a counsellor can help, and a pastor or a friend you trust can stand with you. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What rules about food, clothes or manners did your family treat as almost sacred?
discuss: The Corban vow looked like devotion and worked as an escape. What are the modern versions of that?
Jesus moves uncleanness from what we touch to what comes from the heart. Is that good news, or harder news?
The woman from Syria takes a hard word and keeps asking. What does her answer teach about prayer?
group.pray: Ask God to give each person a clean heart, and pray for anyone in the group who carries thoughts they are ashamed of.

sessions.title: You are the Christ
teaching: Chapter 8 feeds a second crowd, four thousand this time and probably on the Gentile side of the lake, with seven baskets left over. Then come three scenes about seeing. The Pharisees demand a sign from heaven and get none. In the boat the disciples worry about having one loaf, and Jesus asks them question after question: don't you see, don't you remember, don't you understand? At Bethsaida a blind man is healed in two stages, first seeing people like trees walking, then everything clearly. Mark sets him here as a picture of the disciples, who see, but blurred.

Then the hinge of the whole book. On the road near Caesarea Philippi, a town full of other gods and of Rome's power, Jesus asks who people say he is, and then who his friends say he is. Peter answers, “You are the Christ” (Mark 8:29). At once Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected and be killed, and after three days rise again. Peter takes him aside to scold him and is rebuked in front of the others. Then Jesus tells the crowd that anyone who wants to come after him must deny himself and take up his cross.

open.label: Mark 8, passage by passage
open.why: Four thousand fed, a blind man healed in two stages, Peter's confession, and the first time Jesus says he must suffer, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Did Jesus claim to be God?
also.why: In the first three Gospels he never says it in so many words. What he does say and do, set out with the objection stated first.

sessions.question: Jesus asks his friends who they say he is. What is your answer today, and does your life agree with it?
sessions.do: Read 8:27-38 and mark the word must in verse 31. Then write down one way you have wanted a Jesus who wins without a cross.

verse.text: “But what about you?” Jesus asked. “Who do you say I am?” Peter answered, “You are the Christ.”

group.open: Who did people around you say Jesus was when you were growing up?
discuss: Why might Mark put a blind man healed in two stages right before Peter's confession?
Peter loved Jesus and still tried to talk him out of the cross. What did he have in mind?
To Jesus' first hearers a cross meant only one thing. What does taking up a cross ask of an ordinary life?
group.pray: Pray that each person would see Jesus clearly, as the blind man did at the second touch, and ask for courage to follow him on his road.

sessions.title: A father's honest prayer
teaching: Chapter 9 climbs a mountain and comes down again. Peter, James and John see Jesus' clothes shine whiter than any launderer could make them, with Moses and Elijah beside him, and a voice from the cloud says, “This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!” (Mark 9:7). The glory doesn't stay on the mountain. It is given so that the disciples will trust the hard words Jesus has just spoken about the cross. On the way down he tells them to keep quiet about it until the Son of Man has risen, and they wonder what rising could mean.

At the foot of the mountain there is a crowd, an argument and a failure. The disciples could not help a boy whose spirit throws him into fire and water. His father asks Jesus to help if he can. Jesus answers that everything is possible for the one who believes, and the father cries out, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). Jesus helps him anyway. Then, on the road again, Jesus speaks of being handed over, and the disciples argue about which of them is the greatest.

open.label: Mark 9, passage by passage
open.why: The glory on the mountain, a father's honest prayer, an argument about greatness, and hard words about stumbling, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Is believing anything on faith irrational?
also.why: Faith as the New Testament means it is trust resting on testimony and evidence. The case against it is stated first.

sessions.question: Can you pray the father's prayer honestly, and which half of it is harder for you to say?
sessions.do: Read 9:14-29 and the note on its hard question, which warns against treating illness as a demon. Then pray the father's prayer once a day this week, in your own words.

verse.text: Immediately the boy’s father cried out, “I do believe; help my unbelief!”

care: If you are a person whose conscience never rests, who keeps checking whether you have really believed, hear John's words: “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things” (1 John 3:20). Such fear can be part of anxiety or a habit of the mind, and that is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust, and if the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is something you have believed and questioned at the same time?
discuss: The voice on the mountain tells the disciples to listen to Jesus. Why does that come right after his hard words about the cross?
The father believed and questioned in the same breath. How should a church treat someone who prays like that?
Right after Jesus speaks of being handed over, the disciples argue about greatness. Where do you see the same pattern today?
group.pray: Leave a minute for each person to bring God a question or a weak place in their faith without anyone answering it, then ask together for help with unbelief.

sessions.title: A ransom for many
teaching: Chapter 10 is still on the road, and the road goes up to Jerusalem. Along the way Jesus is asked about divorce and answers from the beginning of Genesis, and Christians read his answer in more than one way, as the note on it sets out. He blesses children the disciples tried to send away. A rich man who has kept the commandments walks away grieving, and Mark says that Jesus looked at him and loved him before he asked anything hard. Then Jesus walks ahead, the disciples amazed and the followers afraid, and for the third time he says what will happen in Jerusalem.

Each time Jesus has spoken of his death, the disciples have missed it, and this time James and John ask for the seats at his right and left in his glory. He asks whether they can drink his cup, then gathers the others and turns greatness upside down: whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all. “For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). The road section closes with a blind beggar who asks for sight, receives it, and follows Jesus along the road.

open.label: Mark 10, passage by passage
open.why: Divorce, children, a rich man, the third warning, James and John, and blind Bartimaeus, each passage explained in plain words.

also.label: Why did Jesus die?
also.why: Six pictures the Bible itself uses for what the cross did, a ransom among them, held together without choosing one over the rest.

sessions.question: James and John asked for glory and Bartimaeus asked for sight. If Jesus asked what you want him to do for you, what would you say?
sessions.do: Read 10:32-52 and set what James and John ask for beside what Bartimaeus asks for. Then find one way to serve this week that no one will notice or thank you for.

verse.text: For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.

care: Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who held the highest seat of honor in your family or workplace, and how did everyone know it?
discuss: Jesus loved the rich man before he asked him to give everything up. How does that change the way you hear the command?
The disciples were amazed and the followers were afraid as Jesus walked ahead to Jerusalem. What does it look like to follow him while afraid?
A ransom is the price paid to set a captive free. What does Mark 10:45 say about who paid it?
group.pray: Give thanks for the one who came to serve, and pray for the grace to serve one person this week without being seen.

sessions.title: The king arrives
teaching: In chapter 11 Jesus comes to Jerusalem at Passover, the feast of freedom, in a city ruled by Rome. He rides in on a young donkey, not a war horse, while people spread their cloaks and branches on the road and shout words from Psalm 118: “Hosanna! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” (Mark 11:9). He goes into the temple, looks around at everything, and leaves, because it is late. From here Mark counts the days, and the book slows down. About a third of it is given to this last week.

The next morning Mark makes another sandwich. Jesus finds a fig tree in leaf with no fruit, though it was not the season for figs, and curses it. He goes into the temple, overturns the tables of the money changers, and says that the house meant for prayer for all the nations has been made a den of robbers. The morning after, the tree has withered. Each story explains the other. The note on the fig tree warns against an old misreading that turned it into a curse on the Jewish people. Mark aims the sign at the temple's leaders in that hour.

open.label: Mark 11, passage by passage
open.why: The king on a colt, the fig tree, the tables overturned, faith that moves mountains, and a question about authority, each explained in plain words.

also.label: The king
also.why: The king through the whole Bible in seven pictures, from the promise to David to a king crowned with thorns.

sessions.question: What kind of king do you want Jesus to be, and would you still welcome him if he came humble instead of strong?
sessions.do: Read 11:12-25 as one story: the tree, the temple, then the tree again. Write one sentence on what the fig tree says about the temple.

verse.text: The ones who went ahead and those who followed were shouting: “Hosanna!” “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!”

care: If you have prayed for someone to be rescued, from illness, from danger, from prison, from death, and the rescue did not come, this chapter does not say your prayer was too weak. The three friends in Daniel said God was able to deliver them, “But even if He does not” (Daniel 3:18), they would still trust him. Grief and confusion at such a loss are not a lack of faith. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What does a city look like when it gets ready to welcome someone important?
discuss: Jesus rides a young donkey into the city. What is he saying by that choice?
Why do you think Mark wraps the fig tree around the scene in the temple?
Jesus ties bold prayer to forgiving others. How have you seen his words about prayer misused, and how would you read them instead?
group.pray: Pray for your own church to be a house of prayer for all people, and give thanks for the king who came gently.

sessions.title: Caesar's coin
teaching: Chapter 12 is a day of questions in the temple courts, and most of them are traps. Jesus begins with a story everyone recognized from Isaiah, a vineyard rented to tenants who beat the owner's servants and kill his beloved son, and the leaders know it is aimed at them. Then Pharisees and Herodians, who agreed on little, ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar. If he says yes, the crowd will think he has sided with Rome. If he says no, he can be reported as a rebel.

He asks for a denarius and whose image is on it, and answers, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s” (Mark 12:17). Christians read that answer in more than one way: as two real spheres, as a claim that everything belongs to God, Caesar included, or as an open answer that leaves the hearers to work it out. All agree that Jesus refused to become the tool of either side. The day goes on with Sadducees who make the resurrection look silly, a scribe who is told he is not far from the kingdom, and a poor widow's two coins.

open.label: Mark 12, passage by passage
open.why: The tenants of the vineyard, Caesar's coin, a question about the resurrection, the greatest commandment and a widow's gift, each explained in plain words.

also.label: Should a Christian follow a political party?
also.why: Keep your convictions, but don't hand your conscience to a party: a short answer that turns the same test on every side.

sessions.question: Where has a political side taken a place in your heart that belongs to God?
sessions.do: Name one issue on which you disagree with your own political side. If you can't find one, ask what that says about where your conscience lives.

verse.text: Then Jesus told them, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” And they marveled at Him.

group.open: Whose image is on the money in your wallet, and what does it say about who is in charge?
discuss: Pharisees and Herodians agreed on little, yet they came together to trap Jesus. Why?
The coin bore Caesar's image. If people bear God's image, what belongs to God?
Jesus told a scribe he was not far from the kingdom. What do you think the scribe still lacked?
group.pray: Pray for those who govern, whichever side they are on, and ask God to keep each person in the group from giving any party what belongs to him alone.

sessions.title: Watch
teaching: In chapter 13 a disciple admires the temple's great stones, and Jesus says every one will be thrown down. Within about forty years it was gone: Rome took Jerusalem in AD 70, and the temple burned. On the Mount of Olives four disciples ask when and what sign, and Jesus begins with a warning: “See to it that no one deceives you” (Mark 13:5). Wars, earthquakes and famines are the beginning of birth pains, not the end. The chapter draws on Daniel for the abomination of desolation and the Son of Man coming with the clouds, and it is one of the hardest in the book.

Faithful Christians read it in more than one way. Some read the coming of the Son of Man as Christ's return at the end of the age, some as the prophets' picture language for the fall of Jerusalem, and some as both. The verse skeptics press hardest is “this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened” (Mark 13:30). Mark keeps beside it the saying that no one knows the day or hour, not even the Son, and then a short story about a doorkeeper told to stay awake. Watch for its four hours of the night in the next two chapters.

open.label: Mark 13, passage by passage
open.why: The temple's fall foretold, birth pains, the abomination, the Son of Man, the fig tree and the doorkeeper, with each reading set out fairly.

also.label: Did Jesus predict the end within a generation?
also.why: Schweitzer's case that Jesus expected the end at once and was wrong, stated first, and the readings careful Christians hold, without choosing a scheme.

sessions.question: When you hear talk about the end of the world, what do you feel first, and what does this chapter ask of you instead?
sessions.do: Read 13:32-37, the doorkeeper. Write down the work you have been given while the master is away, and one way to be awake in it this week.

verse.text: And what I say to you, I say to everyone: Keep watch!

group.open: Have you ever been taught a date or a timetable for the end of the world? What did it do to you?
discuss: Jesus' first word to his disciples here is about not being deceived. Why might deception be a greater danger than disaster?
Christians read the coming of the Son of Man in more than one way. What do all the readings share?
In the story, keeping watch means each servant doing his own work. What does that look like on an ordinary Tuesday?
group.pray: Pray for each person's ordinary work this week, that they would be found faithful in it, and give thanks that the future is in God's hands.

sessions.title: The table and the garden
teaching: Chapter 14 sets two gifts side by side. In Bethany a woman breaks a jar of perfume worth nearly a year's wages and pours it on Jesus' head, and he says she has anointed his body ahead of time for burial. Then Judas goes to the chief priests to hand him over. At the Passover meal Jesus says one of them will betray him, and each disciple asks, “Surely not I?” (Mark 14:19). Then he takes bread and a cup and tells them what the food means: his body, and his blood of the covenant, poured out for many.

In Gethsemane Jesus prays with the family word for father, “Abba, Father” (Mark 14:36), asks for the cup to pass, and gives his will to his Father's, while his friends fall asleep three times. The hours of the night from the doorkeeper's story come round one by one. Judas arrives with a kiss, everyone runs, and a young man slips out of his linen cloth and flees. Inside, Jesus answers the high priest plainly. Outside, Peter warms himself by a fire and denies him three times, and when the rooster crows he breaks down and weeps.

open.label: Mark 14, passage by passage
open.why: The perfume, the Passover room, bread and cup, Gethsemane, the arrest, the trial and Peter's denial, each passage explained in plain words.

also.label: Baptism and the Lord's Supper
also.why: What every church shares in the meal Jesus gave that night, and where faithful churches differ, set out without taking a side.

sessions.question: Each disciple asked whether it might be him. When you read of Judas and Peter, do you ask how they could, or whether you could?
sessions.do: Read 14:32-42 slowly. Pray both halves of Jesus' prayer this week, the honest request and the honest surrender, about one thing you are carrying.

verse.text: “Abba, Father,” He said, “all things are possible for You. Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will.”

group.open: What is the most costly gift you have ever seen someone give?
discuss: Mark sets the woman with the perfume right beside Judas. What does each of them give, and for what?
Jesus gave his friends the meal knowing they would fail him within hours. What does that say about who the table is for?
Peter meant his promise and broke it before morning. What is the difference between sincerity and strength?
group.pray: Give thanks for the meal Jesus gave his friends, and pray for anyone in the group who feels they have failed him, that they would know he has not dropped them.

sessions.title: The cross
teaching: Chapter 15 counts the hours. In the morning the council hands Jesus over to Pilate, the Roman governor, who asks whether he is the King of the Jews. A crowd stirred up by the chief priests asks for Barabbas instead, and Pilate, wanting to satisfy them, has Jesus flogged and handed over to be crucified. The note on that scene says plainly that it was never a verdict on the Jewish people. Soldiers dress Jesus in purple and kneel in mock worship, and every part of their joke is true. Of the pain Mark writes only, “And they crucified Him” (Mark 15:24).

At noon darkness covers the land. At three Jesus cries out the first line of Psalm 22, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Mark 15:34), a psalm that begins in the depths and ends in praise. He breathes his last, the temple curtain is torn from top to bottom, the same word Mark used for the heavens torn open at the baptism, and a Roman centurion becomes the first human being in the book to say it: “Truly this man was the Son of God!” (Mark 15:39). The women who followed him from Galilee watch, and see where he is laid.

open.label: Mark 15, passage by passage
open.why: Pilate, Barabbas, the soldiers' mockery, the crucifixion, the cry, the torn curtain and the burial, each passage explained in plain words.

also.label: Sacrifice and the Lamb
also.why: Sacrifice through the whole Bible in seven pictures, from the first covering to the Lamb on the throne.

also.label: Pray Psalm 22
also.why: The psalm Jesus prayed from the cross, which begins in the depths and ends in praise. Choose ‘Pray it slowly’ to take it a part at a time.

sessions.question: The centurion saw how Jesus died and called him the Son of God. What do you see when you look at the cross?
sessions.do: Read Psalm 22 all the way through, the way Mark's first readers would have heard it behind Jesus' cry. Write down the verse where the psalm turns.

verse.text: When the centurion standing there in front of Jesus saw how He had breathed His last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”

care: If you are suffering now, your pain is real, and you are not failing God by feeling it. The psalms are full of people who cried out to God. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). Please do not carry it alone: talk to someone you trust, a friend, a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. The site's Honest Answer, ‘If God is good, why is there so much suffering?’, faces the larger question.

group.open: Where have you seen someone stay with a person in their worst hour?
discuss: Pilate knew Jesus was innocent and gave in to the crowd. Where are you tempted to do the easy thing instead of the right one?
Jesus prayed the first line of a psalm that ends in praise. Do you hear his cry as abandonment, as faith in the dark, or both?
Why do you think the first human being in Mark to call Jesus the Son of God is a Roman soldier at the cross?
group.pray: Give thanks for what Jesus carried, and pray for anyone in the group who feels forsaken, that they would know Jesus prayed that prayer first.

sessions.title: The empty tomb, and Mark's ending
teaching: Early on the first day of the week three women come to finish a burial, and they find the stone rolled back and a young man in white, who says, “He has risen! He is not here!” (Mark 16:6). He sends them to tell the disciples and Peter, named on purpose, that Jesus is going ahead of them into Galilee. In the two oldest complete Bibles that survive, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, copied in the 300s, the book ends two verses later: the women run from the tomb trembling, and in their fear they say nothing to anyone.

Most later manuscripts add verses 9 to 20, which were known by about 180. Most scholars think another hand added them early, and a minority defends them as Mark's own. Some think Mark meant to stop at verse 8 and others that his last page was lost, and nothing in the longer ending is needed for any Christian belief. Either way, the news is already plain in verse 6, and the women's silence did not last, or no one would have heard it. Mark stops at the edge of the story, with a promise of Galilee, where it began, and leaves the next step with whoever has read this far.

open.label: Mark 16, passage by passage
open.why: The women at the tomb, the young man's message, and the longer ending, with what the manuscripts show set out plainly.

also.label: Passages not in the earliest Bibles
also.why: The ending of Mark and the other famous passages missing from the oldest copies, with the evidence on both sides and what it means for the rest.

also.label: The Apostles' Creed
also.why: The oldest summary of the faith still in use, with notes on each line: crucified, buried, and on the third day risen.

sessions.question: The women were afraid and said nothing. What keeps you quiet about what you have seen in this book?
sessions.do: Go back to Mark 1 and begin the book again this week, a chapter a day, reading it in the light of the ending. Write down one thing you see now that you missed the first time.

verse.text: But go, tell His disciples and Peter, ‘He is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see Him, just as He told you.’

care: If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Which of these sixteen sessions will you remember longest, and why?
discuss: The first word of Easter in Mark is for people who failed, Peter by name. What does that say about who the news is for?
If Mark ended at verse 8 on purpose, what might he want the reader to do with the women's silence?
The young man sends the disciples back to Galilee. What would it mean to read the whole book again from the beginning?
group.pray: Give thanks by name for each person in the group, and ask that each would carry what they have seen in Mark into the week ahead.
